# Cholelithiasis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the gallbladder and biliary tract > Cholelithiasis*

[Original Article Link](/library/V30Ghf)

---

## Summary

Cholelithiasis refers to the presence of abnormal concretions (<u>gallstones</u>) in the <u>gallbladder</u>. About 10–20% of American adults have <u>gallstones</u>. <u>Gallstones</u> most commonly consist of <u>cholesterol</u> but may be pigmented (due to <u>hemolysis</u> or infection) or mixed. Cholelithiasis can manifest with <u>biliary colic</u> (<u>postprandial</u> <u>RUQ</u> <u>pain</u>) but is most commonly an incidental finding in asymptomatic individuals. The diagnosis is confirmed by <u>ultrasound</u>. <u>Symptomatic cholelithiasis</u> is managed with <u>laparoscopic cholecystectomy</u>.




See also “<u>Choledocholithiasis</u>,” “<u>Acute cholecystitis</u>,” and “<u>Acute cholangitis</u>.”

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (2–3:1)

* <u>Prevalence</u>: approx. 10–20% of the adult population in developed countries

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: : > 40 years





References: [[1]](/library/s0athQ)[[2]](/library/9lYN_6)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### General




* Imbalance in <u>bile salts</u>, lecithin (stabilizer), <u>cholesterol</u>, <u>calcium carbonate</u>, and <u>bilirubin</u>

* Biliary stasis is a key component in <u>gallstone</u> formation.

* Impaired <u>gallbladder</u> emptying (e.g., due to bowel rest, prolonged <u>total parenteral nutrition</u>, <u>pregnancy</u>;  ) → <u>biliary sludge</u> → <u>bile</u> stasis (<u>cholestasis</u>)





### Cholesterol stones [[1]](/library/s0athQ)[[2]](/library/9lYN_6)




* <u>Risk factors</u>

* <u>Obesity</u>, <u>insulin resistance</u>, <u>dyslipidemia</u>

* Female sex

* Especially during reproductive years due to increased levels of <u>estrogen</u> and <u>progesterone</u>

* Increased <u>estrogen</u> levels cause increased secretion of <u>bile</u> rich in <u>cholesterol</u>, (lithogenic <u>bile</u>), which can result in the formation of <u>cholesterol gallstones</u>.

* Increased <u>progesterone</u> levels cause <u>smooth muscle</u> relaxation, decreased <u>gallbladder</u> contraction, and subsequent <u>bile</u> stasis with formation of <u>gallstones</u>.

* <u>Multiparity</u> or <u>pregnancy</u>

* Age (> 40 years of age)

* European, Native American, or Hispanic ancestry

* <u>Family history</u>

* Drugs: <u>fibrates</u> (inhibition of <u>cholesterol 7-α hydroxylase</u>), <u>estrogen</u> therapy, <u>oral contraceptives</u>

* <u>Malabsorption</u> (e.g., <u>Crohn disease</u>, <u>ileal</u> resection, <u>cystic fibrosis</u>)

* Rapid weight loss (e.g., after <u>bariatric surgery</u>)

* Pathophysiology: abnormal hepatic <u>cholesterol metabolism</u> → ↑ <u>cholesterol</u> concentration in <u>bile</u> and ↓ <u>bile</u> salts and lecithin → hypersaturated <u>bile</u> → precipitation of <u>cholesterol</u> and <u>calcium carbonate</u> → <u>cholesterol stones</u> or <u>mixed stones</u>





> [!NOTE]
> During <u>pregnancy</u>, increased <u>estrogen</u> levels cause increased secretion of lithogenic <u>bile</u> (rich in <u>cholesterol</u>), resulting in the formation of <u>cholesterol gallstones</u>. Increased <u>progesterone</u> levels cause <u>smooth muscle</u> relaxation, decreased and impaired <u>gallbladder</u> contraction, and subsequent <u>bile</u> stasis and formation of <u>gallstones</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Rule of the 6 Fs: Fat, Female, Fertile, Forty, Fair-skinned, Family history.




### Black pigment stones [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[3]](/library/tlYXA6)[[4]](/library/fUYkco)




* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Chronic <u>hemolytic anemias</u> (e.g., <u>sickle cell disease</u>, <u>hereditary spherocytosis</u>)

* (Alcoholic) <u>cirrhosis</u>

* <u>Crohn disease</u>

* <u>Total parenteral nutrition</u>

* Advanced age

* Pathophysiology: ↑ <u>hemolysis</u> → increase in circulating <u>unconjugated bilirubin</u> → increased uptake and conjugation of <u>bilirubin</u> → precipitation of <u>bilirubin</u> polymers and stone formation





### Mixed/brown pigment stones [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[3]](/library/tlYXA6)[[4]](/library/fUYkco)[[5]](/library/80aO3Q)




* <u>Risk factors</u>: bacterial infections and <u>parasites</u> (e.g., <u>Clonorchis sinensis</u>, Opisthorchis species) in the <u>biliary tract</u>, <u>sclerosing</u> <u>cholangitis</u> [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)

* Pathophysiology: infection or <u>infestation</u> → release of <u>β-glucuronidase</u> (by injured <u>hepatocytes</u> and bacteria) → <u>hydrolyzes</u> <u>conjugated bilirubin</u> and lecithin in the <u>bile</u> → increased <u>unconjugated bilirubin</u> and <u>fatty acids</u> → precipitation of <u>calcium carbonate</u>, <u>cholesterol</u>, and <u>calcium</u> bilirubinate (dark color) in <u>bile</u>

## Clinical features

* Most <u>gallstones</u> are asymptomatic.

* Biliary colic: constant, dull <u>RUQ</u> <u>pain</u> lasting < 6 hours 

* Especially <u>postprandial</u>: <u>vagal</u> stimulation (e.g., <u>cholecystokinin</u> release following a fatty meal) → <u>gallbladder</u> contraction → attempts to force the stone into the <u>cystic duct</u>

* May radiate to the epigastrium, right shoulder, and back (<u>referred pain</u>)

* Nonspecific symptoms

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, early satiety

* <u>Bloating</u>, <u>dyspepsia</u>

* <u>Complications of cholelithiasis</u> can be the first manifestation of <u>gallstone disease</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Only a minority of patients with <u>gallstones</u> are symptomatic!

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)




See “<u>Cholelithiasis in pregnancy</u>” for considerations in pregnant individuals.




* Asymptomatic cholelithiasis : No diagnostic workup is required.

* Suspected <u>symptomatic cholelithiasis</u>

* Obtain imaging for cholelithiasis: <u>biliary point-of-care ultrasound</u> (<u>POCUS</u>) or transabdominal <u>RUQ</u> <u>ultrasound</u>

* Rule out <u>complications of cholelithiasis</u> (e.g., <u>acute cholecystitis</u> or <u>choledocholithiasis</u>).

* If the diagnosis remains unclear: See “<u>Diagnosis of acute abdominal pain</u>.”





![Management of cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis](media/nm2t7uayqlp2olwh2dgrgj1a.jpg)

Management of cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis




### Laboratory studies for suspected cholelithiasis




<u>Laboratory studies</u> are typically normal in uncomplicated cholelithiasis but should be ordered to rule out other acute biliary conditions and/or other causes of <u>acute abdominal pain</u>.




* <u>CBC</u>: usually normal

* <u>LFTs</u>: usually normal

* <u>Amylase</u>, <u>lipase</u>: usually normal





> [!TIP]
> <u>Laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>WBC count</u>, <u>LFTs</u>, <u>lipase</u>, <u>amylase</u>) are usually normal in uncomplicated cholelithiasis.




### RUQ ultrasound for suspected cholelithiasis




If appropriately trained, consider performing a <u>biliary POCUS</u>.




* Indication: best initial test in suspected <u>symptomatic cholelithiasis</u>   [[6]](/library/9IYNUq)[[7]](/library/SgbyuG)

* Characteristic findings [[6]](/library/9IYNUq)

* Cholelithiasis [[8]](/library/hgbcEG)

* Intraluminal highly echogenic foci

* Strong <u>posterior acoustic shadowing</u>

* <u>Rolling stone sign</u>: movement of the echogenic foci with the changing of patient posture

* Biliary sludge  [[9]](/library/3gbSEG)[[10]](/library/RgblEG)[[11]](/library/CgbqxG)

* Low-level echogenic material in the dependent portion of the GB

* No <u>posterior acoustic shadowing</u>

* Slow movement with the changing of patient posture

* <u>Accuracy</u>: operator- and technique-dependent [[12]](/library/k8cm5V0)

* <u>RUQ</u> <u>ultrasound</u> performed by a radiologist: ≥ 95% <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u> for cholelithiasis

* <u>Biliary POCUS</u> performed by emergency providers: ∼ 90% <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u> for cholelithiasis





> [!TIP]
> If appropriately trained, consider performing a <u>biliary POCUS</u> to rule in cholelithiasis. If the study is negative, further investigations (e.g., <u>laboratory studies</u>, <u>RUQ</u> <u>ultrasound</u> performed by a radiologist, additional imaging) may be necessary. [[12]](/library/k8cm5V0)

### Additional imaging studies




Additional imaging may be required if <u>complications of cholelithiasis</u> (e.g., <u>acute cholecystitis</u>, <u>acute cholangitis</u>, <u>choledocholithiasis</u>, <u>biliary pancreatitis</u>) cannot be ruled out, or to evaluate for other causes of abdominal <u>pain</u>.




#### <u>MRI</u> abdomen without and with IV contrast with <u>MRCP</u> [[6]](/library/9IYNUq)




* Indications

* Preferred second-line test if <u>ultrasound</u> findings are inconclusive

* Suspected <u>choledocholithiasis</u>  (see ''Diagnostics'' in <u>choledocholithiasis</u> for further details)

* Supportive findings: well-defined <u>hypointense</u> (on T2) filling defect(s) within the <u>gallbladder</u> lumen [[13]](/library/rgbf9G)





#### CT abdomen with IV contrast  [[6]](/library/9IYNUq)




* Indications

* Inconclusive <u>ultrasound</u> findings; <u>MRI</u> is not available

* Suspected complications and/or differential diagnoses

* Preoperative planning after confirming the diagnosis

* Supportive findings (of <u>radiopaque</u> stones): well-defined <u>hyperdense</u> structure(s) within the <u>gallbladder</u> lumen

* Disadvantages

* Only <u>radiopaque</u> stones are detectable (15–20% of stones are <u>radiopaque</u>).  [[14]](/library/DYb1rH)[[15]](/library/Xib9Jt)

* Cannot detect the more common <u>radiolucent</u> pure <u>cholesterol stones</u>





![Cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis](media/x67904nhq856f0sa0vbrry0u.jpg)

Cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis




#### <u>Abdominal x-ray</u>




* Indication: usually not indicated in the evaluation of cholelithiasis, but may be performed as part of the workup of <u>acute abdominal pain</u>

* Findings: <u>gallstones</u> with an outer <u>radiopaque</u> rim and <u>radiolucent</u> center [[16]](/library/R-clCU0)

* Disadvantages: similar to those of <u>CT scan</u>





![Gallbladder calculi](media/qzzaqug4b8ll76u64444nn0e.jpg)

Gallbladder calculi




> [!TIP]
> <u>X-ray</u> and <u>CT scan</u> are rarely diagnostic in cholelithiasis because only 15–20% of stones are <u>radiopaque</u>. Pure <u>cholesterol stones</u> are <u>radiolucent</u>.

## Differential diagnoses

### Differential diagnosis of <u>RUQ</u> <u>pain</u>




* Abdominal (See also “<u>Acute abdominal pain</u>” and “<u>Differential diagnosis of abdominal pain</u>.”)

* <u>Choledocholithiasis</u>

* <u>Acute cholecystitis</u>

* <u>Acute cholangitis</u>

* Acute <u>hepatic capsule</u> swelling (e.g., acute <u>hepatitis</u>, <u>perihepatitis</u>, <u>congestive hepatopathy</u>)

* <u>Gastroesophageal reflux</u>, <u>gastritis</u>, <u>gastrointestinal ulcers</u>

* Early <u>appendicitis</u>

* <u>Acute pancreatitis</u>

* Right-sided <u>diverticulitis</u>

* <u>Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction</u>

* Extra-abdominal

* <u>Nephrolithiasis</u>

* <u>Acute coronary syndrome</u> (See also “<u>Chest pain</u>.”)

* See also “<u>Differential diagnosis of acute abdomen</u>.”





### Differential diagnoses of intraluminal <u>gallbladder</u> wall pathology




* <u>Cholangiocarcinoma</u>

* <u>Gallbladder polyp</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

## Treatment

### Approach  [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[18]](/library/2EYTEI)[[19]](/library/wgbhxG)




See “<u>Cholelithiasis in pregnancy</u>” for considerations in pregnant individuals.




* Asymptomatic cholelithiasis

* <u>Expectant management</u> is typically sufficient.

* Consider the need for prophylactic <u>cholecystectomy</u>: See “Indications” in “Surgical Management.”

* Patients with <u>gallstones</u> found incidentally during an ED visit can be referred back to their primary care physician for <u>shared decision-making</u> regarding surgical consult.

* Symptomatic uncomplicated cholelithiasis

* Treatment of biliary colic

* Provide <u>initial supportive therapy for acute biliary disease</u>.

* Counsel on lifestyle modifications to prevent further attacks (see “<u>Nonoperative management of cholelithiasis</u>” for details.)

* Outpatient referral to general <u>surgery</u> for an elective <u>cholecystectomy</u> to prevent recurrence.

* Consider surgical consult and admission if the <u>pain</u> is intractable.

* Symptomatic <u>complicated cholelithiasis</u>

* Admit for further management and consult general <u>surgery</u> and/or gastroenterology.

* See “<u>Acute cholecystitis</u>,” “<u>Acute cholangitis</u>,” “<u>Choledocholithiasis</u>,” and “<u>Biliary pancreatitis</u>.”





![Management of cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis](media/nm2t7uayqlp2olwh2dgrgj1a.jpg)

Management of cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis




### Initial supportive therapy of acute biliary disease [[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[19]](/library/wgbhxG)




* Bowel rest: <u>NPO</u>

* In <u>biliary colic</u>: until the <u>pain</u> subsides (typically within a few hours)  [[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)

* In other acute biliary conditions: The duration of <u>NPO</u> depends on the need for urgent interventional therapy

* <u>Analgesics</u> [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)

* <u>NSAIDs</u>: preferred first-line <u>analgesics</u>  [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[20]](/library/YJYnsJ)[[21]](/library/glbFwF)

* <u>Ketorolac</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Diclofenac</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Ibuprofen</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Opioids</u>: for severe <u>pain</u> that does not improve with <u>NSAIDs</u> or in patients with <u>contraindications to NSAIDs</u>  [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[22]](/library/olb0BF)

* <u>Morphine</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Buprenorphine</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[23]](/library/HgbK9G)

* <u>Meperidine</u> DOSAGE [[24]](/library/0JYesJ)[[25]](/library/aJYQsJ)

* See also “<u>Pain management</u>.”

* <u>Spasmolytics</u> (e.g., <u>dicyclomine</u> DOSAGE): consider as <u>adjuvant therapy</u> with <u>analgesics</u> in patients with severe <u>pain</u> [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)

* Treatment for protracted <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>IV fluid therapy</u>

* <u>Antiemetics</u>

* Consider <u>NG tube insertion</u> with suction.





### Surgical management




* Procedure: elective <u>laparoscopic cholecystectomy</u>

* Indications

* Symptomatic cholelithiasis

* Asymptomatic cholelithiasis with any of the following:

* Increased risk of <u>gallbladder cancer</u> (e.g., <u>gallbladder polyps</u>, <u>porcelain gallbladder</u>, <u>gallstones</u> ≥ 3 cm) [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[26]](/library/xgbExG)

* Increased risk of developing complications (e.g., <u>immunocompromised</u> patients, multiple <u>gallstones</u>) [[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[18]](/library/2EYTEI)

* Increased risk of becoming symptomatic (e.g., <u>hemolytic anemia</u>, patients undergoing <u>gastric bypass surgery</u>)  [[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[27]](/library/BgbzxG)[[28]](/library/ygbdBG)

* Contraindication: suspected <u>gallbladder cancer</u> (see ''Treatment'' in “<u>Biliary cancer</u>”)  [[18]](/library/2EYTEI)[[29]](/library/_gb5BG)

* Preoperative precautions: Assess for <u>predictors of choledocholithiasis</u> in all symptomatic patients (see ''<u>Diagnosis of choledocholithiasis</u>”).   [[30]](/library/wlYh_6)

* Timing: as early as possible in uncomplicated <u>symptomatic cholelithiasis</u>  [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)[[31]](/library/zgbrBG)[[32]](/library/ZSbZyG)

* Complications: See “<u>Complications of cholecystectomy</u>”.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Cholecystectomy</u> is usually not indicated in asymptomatic cholelithiasis.




### Nonoperative management of cholelithiasis [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)




#### Indications




* Patients at high risk of complications due to <u>surgery</u> or anesthesia (e.g., recent <u>myocardial infarction</u>)

* Patients unwilling to undergo <u>surgery</u>





#### <u>Expectant management</u> [[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)




* Lifestyle modifications :

* Low-fat diet (especially low in saturated fats)  [[33]](/library/YSbnyG)

* Avoid lithogenic drugs, such as <u>estrogen</u>, <u>fibrates</u>. [[34]](/library/0SbeyG)

* Exercise regularly.

* Follow-up: if symptoms recur





#### Oral <u>bile acid</u> dissolution therapy




* May be useful in dissolving pure <u>cholesterol stones</u> (i.e., <u>radiolucent</u> stones) that are < 0.5 cm [[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)

* <u>Ursodeoxycholic acid</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE

* Duration of therapy: 6–24 months [[17]](/library/nJY7uJ)[[33]](/library/YSbnyG)

* Advantage: symptomatic improvement even if stones are not completely dissolved [[33]](/library/YSbnyG)

* Disadvantages

* Ineffective in <u>mixed stones</u>

* High recurrence rates  [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)

* Long duration of therapy

* Requires repeat imaging to track treatment response





#### Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (<u>ESWL</u>)




<u>ESWL</u> is also used in the <u>treatment of nephrolithiasis</u>.




* Definition: : a noninvasive method of stone fragmentation using an acoustic <u>pulse</u> in the treatment of <u>gallstones</u> and <u>pancreatic</u> stones

* Indication: typically used for solitary stones that can be localized well on imaging (<u>radiolucent</u>)

* Procedure

* Stones are localized using <u>x-ray</u> or <u>ultrasound</u>.

* A lithotriptor generates <u>shock waves</u> that are focused on the stone, fragmenting it in the process.

* Passage of stone fragments

* Biliary stones: through the <u>biliary system</u> into the <u>duodenum</u>.

* <u>Pancreatic</u> stones: through the <u>pancreatic duct</u> into the <u>duodenum</u>

* Advantage: is noninvasive:  and can be performed on an outpatient basis  [[2]](/library/9lYN_6)

* Disadvantages

* Commonly causes <u>biliary colic</u>

* Lower success rate in the presence of multiple stones

* Risk of injury to adjacent solid organs (rare)

* Prognosis: high recurrence rate (between 40 and 60% within 5 years) [[35]](/library/MicMHX0)[[36]](/library/nic7HX0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>ESWL</u> is contraindicated in <u>pregnancy</u>. [[37]](/library/qOdCtJ0)

---

## Complications

### General




* <u>Cholecystitis</u>

* <u>Acute cholecystitis</u> (most common)

* <u>Chronic cholecystitis</u>

* <u>Porcelain gallbladder</u>

* <u>Choledocholithiasis</u>

* <u>Acute cholangitis</u>

* Acute <u>biliary pancreatitis</u>

* <u>Biliary-enteric fistula</u>: Cholecystoenteric/<u>choledochoenteric fistula</u> (rare) , which can cause <u>gallstone ileus</u> (rare)  [[47]](/library/mSbVZt)[[48]](/library/5SbiZt)

### Complications due to <u>gallstone</u> impaction at the <u>gallbladder</u> neck or infundibulum




#### Mirizzi syndrome [[49]](/library/lSbv-G)[[50]](/library/NSb--G)




* Definition: extrinsic compression of the <u>common bile duct</u> (or any extrahepatic <u>bile</u> duct) by <u>gallstone</u>(s) impacted in the <u>cystic duct</u> or the infundibulum of the <u>gallbladder</u>  [[49]](/library/lSbv-G)[[51]](/library/OSbI-G)

* Clinical features: similar to <u>choledocholithiasis</u>

* Diagnostics: preferably <u>ERCP</u>/<u>MRCP</u>

* Narrowing of the <u>common hepatic duct</u>

* Stone within the <u>cystic duct</u>

* Dilation of the intrahepatic biliary tree

* Treatment

* <u>ERCP</u>-guided <u>CBD</u> <u>stent</u> placement may be considered preoperatively to allow for biliary drainage. [[52]](/library/-hbDgt)

* <u>Open cholecystectomy</u> may be preferred if diagnosed preoperatively.  [[50]](/library/NSb--G)

* Complications [[53]](/library/rQbfxt)[[54]](/library/3jbSZF)

* Cholecystocholedochal <u>fistula</u>: an abnormal communication between the <u>gallbladder</u> and the <u>common bile duct</u>

* Cholecystoenteric/<u>choledochoenteric fistula</u> (<u>biliary-enteric fistula</u>): an abnormal communication between the <u>gallbladder</u> or the <u>CBD</u> with the adjacent bowel

* <u>Gallstone ileus</u>: due to <u>biliary-enteric fistula</u>





#### Gallbladder mucocele (<u>gallbladder hydrops</u>) [[47]](/library/mSbVZt)[[55]](/library/zbbrwH)




* Definition: marked distention of the <u>gallbladder</u> with sterile <u>mucinous</u> content due to chronic biliary outflow obstruction

* Etiology [[55]](/library/zbbrwH)

* Impacted <u>gallstone</u> at the <u>gallbladder</u> neck (most common)

* Resolved <u>acute cholecystitis</u> [[47]](/library/mSbVZt)

* Tumors at the <u>gallbladder</u> neck or <u>CBD</u> (e.g., GB polyps, <u>cholangiocarcinoma</u>, <u>carcinoma</u> of <u>pancreatic</u> head)

* Acute inflammatory conditions (e.g., <u>Kawasaki disease</u>)

* Extrinsic compression of the biliary outflow tract (e.g., <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, adhesions, strictures)

* Pathophysiology: chronic biliary outflow obstruction → resorption of <u>bile</u> and secretion of <u>mucin</u> by biliary <u>mucosa</u> → collection of <u>mucinous</u> secretion within the <u>gallbladder</u> with no outflow → gross distention of the <u>gallbladder</u>

* Clinical features: asymptomatic mass in the <u>RUQ</u>; no signs of infection

* Diagnostics: (preferably <u>ultrasound</u> or CT); show grossly distended fluid-filled <u>gall bladder</u> without signs of inflammation [[55]](/library/zbbrwH)

* Treatment

* In children with no evidence of <u>cholecystitis</u>: trial of <u>conservative management</u>  [[56]](/library/MSbMZt)

* In adults: <u>laparoscopic cholecystectomy</u> [[55]](/library/zbbrwH)
